summary: An inherited review-wait ledger was unretirable by construction, and the recovery route that creates the wedge is the same one required to take the item over. The wait entry's claimGeneration named a claim-marker comment that no longer existed, and ReviewWait.project compares the STORED receipt's generation against the LIVE claim - so timeout, cancel and complete were all refused with 'entry receipt claimGeneration is not current' regardless of which generation the event supplied, while a fresh enter was refused with 'a preceding reviewGeneration is still unconsumed'. The trap is that a dead holder can only be displaced by claim --force, which mints a new generation and thereby guarantees the mismatch: any inheriting worker converts a merely-expired wait into an unretirable one by the act of inheriting it. Recovery required preserving the entry verbatim and deleting it. Recorded because the before/after oracle pair is the only thing that distinguishes this from a false exhaustion.

A committed gate-inversion harness that nothing invokes is a record, not a gate - the exact failure its own header warns about. scripts/test-working-set-gate-mutations.sh shipped referenced by zero call sites while the repository's equivalent, scripts/test-spatial-subject-mutations.sh, has three. The proof that three new fixtures can fail therefore ran once, by hand, and would not have re-run when a later refactor reshaped the literals the mutations match - which is precisely how a mutation harness goes vacuous. Wired into verify-spatial-query.sh's serial direct route; NOT into the concurrent prepared-PR route, because unlike the existing harness this one mutates sources in the working tree rather than in an isolated mutant directory, so the CI route needs that isolation first.

Re-measuring against a moved base is the right instinct, and I drew a false cause from it. I reported F4's win dropping 3.5x -> 2.9x and attributed it to the rebase onto a main 62 commits newer. The rebase cannot have moved it: measure-working-set.sh swaps exactly two files and both carry identical blob ids at the old and new bases, last touched 190 commits earlier - the baseline did not move at all. The 2.9x was a LOAD ARTIFACT, from running the harness in the background while other work occupied the machine; only its after side was inflated. Serialized on a quiet machine across three independent runs the figure is 3.60x with a 3% across-run swing, and the original 3.5x was substantially right. The compounding error was the stability bound: I derived it from spread WITHIN one run, where every round shares the same machine load and therefore agrees while being jointly wrong. Within-run agreement is not reproducibility. A restated number needs the across-run spread and a quiet machine, or it is just a differently-wrong number with more confidence attached.

A before/after harness silently degenerated into measuring one side against itself, twice, and reported it as success: three successive runs gave 3.56x, then 0.99x, then 1.01x with a valid base and genuinely differing sources. Cause: restore() used 'cp -p', so sources came back with mtimes older than existing build outputs and the next incremental build handed back the previous side's assembly. The failure mode is the dangerous direction - uniform ~1.00x reads as 'no regression' rather than as 'no measurement'. WHAT CLOSES IT IS A MITIGATION, NOT A DETECTOR: touching the sources before each build makes them newer than any output, so the build cannot skip. I first recorded that the assembly-digest guard was what caught it. That was false, and the reason is a property of the ground rather than of my code: this toolchain does not GUARANTEE reproducible output, so digest inequality carries no information - my own recorded provenance shows three digests for one immutable blob, while five consecutive rebuilds of an unchanged source agreed. Not stable enough to mean 'different', not unstable enough to notice. Digest EQUALITY does carry information (two identical assemblies from two different sources means a skipped build) and that case is refused and self-tested. The transferable rule: state a guard at the strength its mechanism delivers. A detector built on an inequality is only as good as the determinism underneath it, and here there is none to build on.

I refused to gate F4 on the grounds that 'neighbours evaluated once per expansion' has no behavioural signature - deterministic pure function, so a duplicate call leaves path, cost, expansions and canonical bytes byte-identical. The refusal to ship a source-text assertion was right; the reason was wrong. ALLOCATION is a signature: the workload allocates 15,656,832 bytes byte-exact across runs, and restoring the duplicate evaluation takes it to 26,831,424 (+71%) while every structural counter stays identical. 'No observable difference' meant 'no difference in the outputs I had thought to look at' - cost is observable too. The gate went into --print-spatial-performance, which verify-spatial-query.sh already runs on BOTH the direct and prepared-PR routes, so it is continuously enforced in CI without touching the contended qualify-pr.sh. The reachable home existed the whole time; I had scoped the search to the files I was already editing.

An anti-vacuity assertion I added in the same change that added the gate turned out to guard nothing, and the shape is worth naming: I strengthened a CLAIM without strengthening the EVIDENCE. The allocation budget was advertised as unable to 'pass vacuously on a query that never reached the fallback loop', enforced by 'expansions > 0'. But boundedPath's FAST path returns 'int32 path.Length' AS its expansion count, so the counter is positive on both routes and separates neither; emptying the wall-dense world took the fast path and passed at 504,896 bytes. The fix is a signal only the fallback can produce - strict 'expansions > path-cells', which the fast path cannot satisfy because it forces equality - plus a pin on the calibrated workload, because a second escape (thinned walls: fallback still entered, 16,343,104 bytes) fits UNDER the ceiling and would have re-baselined the budget silently. Lesson: when adding an assertion whose job is to prove another assertion is not vacuous, invert the anti-vacuity assertion itself. I inverted the budget and not its guard.

DOTNET_ROOT_X64 was live in this shell (=/usr/share/dotnet) alongside DOTNET_ROOT (=~/.dotnet), and the two roots carry DIFFERENT runtimes - 10.0.11 and 10.0.10. Measurements here happened to be safe because the muxer on PATH is the ~/.dotnet apphost, which resolves from its own location, so both sides traced to 10.0.10 - but that is luck, not a property anything enforced. A before/after comparison split across two runtimes attributes a runtime difference to the code change. The harness now records the framework each side actually loaded and refuses when they disagree (exit 9), self-tested in both directions by diverting one side to the other root. Worth contrasting with the assembly digest in the same script: a framework version is a MEANINGFUL identity, so equality and inequality both inform, whereas a non-reproducible build digest only informs on equality. Same script, two guards, deliberately different strengths.
